objectives: Explain what a credit card is and when it starts costing you money.
Work out how a billing cycle turns purchases into a bill and a due date.
Compare an interest rate, an APR and a daily rate.
Calculate what paying only the minimum payment really costs.
Spot the four traps that cost the most: cash advances, balance transfers, late payments and closed accounts.
Read a statement in ten minutes and find the four numbers that matter.
Ask a bank for a lower rate using sentences you can copy.

sections.body:
A credit card is a promise to pay later. When you swipe it in a shop, you are not buying the item with money you already have. You are asking the bank to pay the shop now and to send you the bill. The bank charges you for that service, either as interest on the balance or as part of the price you already paid for the card.

The card has four parts that matter. The **credit limit** is the most the bank will let you borrow at one time. The **billing cycle** is the period between two statements. The **interest rate** is the price of borrowing, usually written as an annual percentage rate, or **APR**. The **minimum payment** is the smallest amount the bank will accept in a month.

That promise has a price, and the price is not hidden. A shop may charge you extra for taking a card, and a card with no annual fee still charges interest when you carry a balance. What makes credit useful is the gap between when you spend and when you pay. That gap is valuable when it is short and managed. It becomes expensive when it is long and unnoticed.

Credit cards also work as a payment tool, not only as a loan. If you pay the full balance every month, you have used the card's payment network and borrowed nothing. That is the cheapest way to use one. Interest appears only when a balance stays on the card beyond the grace period.

Everything in this article follows from that one fact: interest is charged on the balance you carry, and a balance you do not carry costs you nothing.
examples: I paid the full balance, so no interest was charged.
The credit limit is the most the bank will let me borrow at one time.
I use the card to pay, not to borrow.
sections.heading: What a credit card actually is

sections.body:
The billing cycle is the engine of the whole system, and it runs whether you look at it or not.

On a given day each month, the bank closes your account and prints a statement. Everything you bought since the previous statement appears on it, together with any interest or fees. That list is the **statement balance**. The statement also carries a **due date**, usually about three weeks later. If you pay the statement balance in full before the due date, no interest is charged on any of those purchases.

Between the statement date and the due date sits the **grace period**. It is not free money, because the money is still yours and you can still be charged if you miss the date. It is a short extension of time at no cost, and it is the reason a card is worth having for ordinary monthly spending.

The number to watch is the difference between the statement balance and the minimum payment. The statement balance is what the purchases cost. The minimum payment is usually the larger of a small percentage of the statement balance, or a small fixed sum, or the interest plus a percentage. If you pay only the minimum, the rest stays on the card and interest is charged on it.

Payments also work in a fixed order. The bank applies your payment to the oldest balance first, then to interest, then to new purchases. This is called the **payment allocation rule**, and it is written into your agreement. It matters because it decides how much of your payment actually reduces the balance you were charged interest on.

Some cards use a daily billing cycle instead of a monthly one. The rule is the same, but the statement arrives every day and the grace period is counted in days rather than from a statement date. Read which one your card uses, because the dates on your calendar will not match otherwise.
examples: The statement balance is what I spent, and the minimum payment is the smallest slice of it.
My grace period runs until the due date, so I pay in full before then.
sections.heading: How one billing cycle works

sections.body:
An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. On a card it is normally charged on the balance, not on the limit, and it is normally charged per day.

The **APR** is the headline number: the annual percentage rate, including most fees, expressed as a yearly figure. A card with a 24 % APR charges roughly 24 % a year, which works out at about 0.066 % a day. Multiply that daily rate by the balance and by the number of days it stays, and you have the interest. Banks usually add interest to the balance, so unpaid interest is charged interest of its own next month.

The card may show you several different rates, and they are not the same rate. The **purchase APR** covers ordinary shopping. A **balance transfer APR** may be lower or free for a fixed promotional period. A **cash advance APR** is higher and often starts immediately. A **penalty APR** is what your rate becomes if you pay late, and it can be higher than the standard rate for the whole balance, not only for the late amount.

The number that matters for comparison is the APR, because it includes most of the cost. A card with a 20 % APR and no annual fee is often cheaper than one with 18 % APR and a 95 $ annual fee, if you keep the card for years.

And a rate is only a price until a balance exists. If you clear the balance every month, the APR never applies. Interest is the price of *not* paying, so the decision is not which card to carry but whether to carry a balance at all.
examples: A 24 % APR is about 0.066 % a day on the balance.
The cash advance rate is higher and it starts on the day I take the money out.
A late payment moved me onto the penalty rate for the whole balance.
sections.heading: What an interest rate means, and what APR means

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet on the plastic and on the statement, and what each one actually does.

**APR** is the annual percentage rate: the yearly price of borrowing, with most fees included. **Interest** is the money actually charged, usually calculated on the balance each day and added to it.

**Credit limit** is the most you may owe at one time. **Available credit** is the limit minus what you already owe. Using most of your available credit is not good for your score even if you always pay on time.

**Billing cycle** is the period between two statements. **Grace period** is the days after the statement date during which you can pay in full without interest. **Statement date** is the day the statement is cut. **Due date** is the day the payment must arrive.

**Minimum payment** is the smallest sum the card will accept. **Previous balance** is what you owed on the last statement. **New balance** is that amount plus new purchases minus payments plus interest.

**Overdue fee** is the charge for paying late. **Annual fee** is the yearly charge for holding the card. **Foreign transaction fee** is the extra cost of using the card abroad. **Cash advance** is money taken out with the card, usually with its own fee and its own rate.

**Payment allocation rule** is the order in which the bank applies your money, and it decides how quickly a balance actually falls.
sections.heading: The words on the card and the statement

terms.example: This card has a 24 % APR, which is about 0.066 % a day.
terms.gloss: The yearly price of borrowing on the card, with most fees included. It is the number to compare two cards by.

terms.example: My credit limit is 2000 $, and I use about 600 $ of it.
terms.gloss: The most the bank will let you borrow on the card at one time. Going over it is usually refused and sometimes charged.

terms.example: The billing cycle closes on the 12th, so my groceries appear on the 12th statement.
terms.gloss: The period between two statements. Everything bought in one cycle appears on the next statement.

terms.example: If I pay the statement balance inside the grace period, I pay no interest.
terms.gloss: The days between the statement date and the due date, during which you can pay in full without interest.

terms.example: The minimum payment is 25 $, so the rest of the balance stays on the card.
terms.gloss: The smallest monthly sum the card will accept. Paying only this keeps the balance, and the interest, alive.

terms.example: The late payment cost me a 35 $ overdue fee and my standard rate went up.
terms.gloss: The charge the bank makes for a late payment, on top of any penalty rate and any loss of your good history.

sections.body:
The minimum payment is the most expensive number on the statement, because it is designed to clear a balance slowly without ever being a repayment plan.

Here is the arithmetic. Suppose you owe 1000 $ on a card with a 24 % APR, and the minimum payment is 25 $ a month. The interest alone is about 20 $ a month on the first month, so only 5 $ of your payment touches the balance. As the balance falls the interest falls with it, but it never falls to nothing. On these numbers the balance is still there after five years, and you will have paid about 1400 $ in total.

Nothing about this is a trick. The card issuer does not lose money, and you keep a usable card with a good history. But a balance held for five years at 24 % costs more than half again what you borrowed.

A second trap sits inside the minimum payment: it is calculated on the balance, so paying less makes the next minimum smaller. The payment shrinks just as slowly as the debt, which keeps you in the same position for longer.

The rule that avoids all of this is simple. **Pay the statement balance in full every month.** If you cannot, treat the card as a short-term loan, and compare the cost of that loan with the cost of a cheaper one: a bank overdraft, a small loan, or a balance transfer with a lower rate. A credit card at 24 % APR is rarely the cheapest way to carry money for months.

Keep one rule next to your card: if a balance is still there after the due date, the card has become a loan, and it should be priced like one.
examples: Paying the minimum keeps the balance alive, so the interest keeps growing.
A 1000 $ balance at 24 % APR takes about five years to clear at 25 $ a month.
I paid the statement balance in full, so this month cost me nothing in interest.
sections.heading: The minimum payment and why it costs so much

sections.body:
**A cash advance** is money taken out with the card. It usually carries a fee of a few percent, a higher rate, and no grace period: the interest starts the same day. Using the card at an ATM is the most common way people get one without meaning to.

**A balance transfer** moves an existing debt onto a card with a lower promotional rate. The transfer fee is often 3 to 5 % of the amount, and when the promotional period ends the rate jumps. Read the end date before you transfer, not after.

**A late payment** costs a fee and, on many cards, moves the whole balance to a penalty APR that is higher than the standard rate. It can also affect your credit history, which decides what you are offered next year.

**Closing an account to stop the charges** often makes things worse. A closed card may still collect its balance, the statement may stop arriving so you miss the due date, and the lost history can lower your limit on the other cards. If you want to stop using a card, keep it, set an alert, and stop putting anything on it.
sections.heading: The four traps that cost the most

sections.body:
The statement is a working document, not an envelope to throw away. Ten minutes with it will tell you your real rate, your real balance and what will happen next month.

Start at the summary box, because every bank puts the four numbers that matter in the same place. Then work down the transaction list, which is the part nobody reads and the part that catches recurring charges you forgot about.

The transaction list is also where you find the truth about your spending habits. A subscription you cancelled but the company kept billing is visible there as a small repeating line. Those are the leaks that quietly cost more than a single large purchase.
examples: There is a 12 $ charge here every month that I did not know about.
I am close to my credit limit, so I will clear this balance before anything else.
sections.heading: Reading your statement in ten minutes
steps: Open the summary box and write down the statement balance, the minimum payment, the due date and the APR.
Check the previous balance against the last statement to see whether it actually came down.
Scan the transaction list for anything you do not recognise.
Circle every recurring charge and confirm you still want it.
Check whether you are close to the credit limit.
Set a payment for the statement balance, not the minimum, and set a reminder two days before the due date.

sections.body:
Cards are advertised on rewards and on the first-purchase discount. Those are the least important numbers. What decides the cost is the rate, the fee and the way you actually use it.

Compare five things. The **APR**, because it is the price of the balance you will carry. The **grace period**, because it decides whether you can pay in full without interest. The **annual fee**, because it is charged whether you use the card or not. The **late fee**, because it is the price of one bad day. The **foreign transaction fee**, if you travel, because it is charged on every purchase abroad.

Then think about your behaviour, not your intentions. If you clear the balance every month, the card that is cheapest for you is the one with no annual fee, a decent grace period and a low rate for the month you do slip. If you expect to carry a balance, the rate dominates and the rewards do not matter. If you travel often, a card with no foreign transaction fee beats a better rewards card every time.

And be careful with introductory rates. A 0 % rate for six months is a discount, not a card. Read what happens after: the standard rate, the annual fee, and whether you must pay the balance in full before the period ends or the remaining amount is charged at the standard rate.

Finally, ask what the issuer wants from you. A bank that needs your balance at 24 % is making money from you keeping a balance, and it will design the offer to keep it there.
examples: This card has no annual fee and a 22 % APR, which suits how I use it.
The promotional rate ends in six months, so I will clear the balance before then.
I travel twice a year, so the foreign transaction fee matters more than the rewards.
sections.heading: Comparing two cards before you apply

sections.body:
If you already carry a balance at a high rate, the goal is one: reduce the balance and the rate at the same time. Everything else is detail.

Start by writing down every balance, the APR on each one, and the minimum payment on each one. Most people find they do not know the rate on their oldest card. Ask each bank for it, or find it on the statement.

Then stop using the cards that carry the balance. Not the card in general: the card with the balance on it. You can keep one card with no balance for ordinary spending, and close the temptation rather than the account.

Next, ask the bank for a lower rate. It is cheap for them to move a customer to a lower rate, because the relationship is worth more than one year's interest on 2000 $. A lower rate on the same balance is free money, and it costs you nothing to ask. If the balance is large, a balance transfer to a lower rate can buy you several months, and you should compare the transfer fee against the interest you save.

Then pay more than the minimum, and aim it deliberately. The **avalanche method** pays the highest rate first, which removes the most interest. The **snowball method** pays the smallest balance first, which is easier to keep up. Pick the one you will actually keep doing.

Make one extra payment a year where you can, and stop adding new charges. Most balances that felt impossible at the start are cleared within two years once the rate comes down and the balance stops growing.
examples: What rate am I paying on this card, and can you lower it?
I have three cards with balances, and this one has the highest rate.
I will pay extra towards the highest rate first, and keep the other card for everyday spending.
sections.heading: Getting out of expensive debt

sections.body:
These are the sentences that get things done on a phone call with a bank. Read them once, adapt the numbers, and keep them somewhere you can find them while you are on hold.

Say the balance and the number you want. Banks move faster when the request is a specific number rather than a complaint. Ask for the thing that costs you money, not for a vague review.

If you are calling about a charge you do not recognise, ask for the date, the amount and the merchant, and ask how to dispute it. If you are calling about a rate, ask for the current rate in writing as well, so you can check the next statement.

And end the call by asking what the bank will do next and when, then note it down. A call you cannot check later is a call that did not happen.
examples: I want to pay down my balance. What rate can you offer me?
There is a charge of 45 $ on the 3rd that I do not recognise. How do I dispute it?
Can you confirm my credit limit in writing?
What is my current APR, and when does the promotional period end?
I am paying this off this month. Is there anything I need to do on my side?
Can you note on the account that I asked for a lower rate today?
sections.heading: Sentences you can use with your bank

item.summary: A credit card is a loan with a billing cycle attached. After reading this you can work out what a balance really costs, why the minimum payment takes years to clear, which card traps cost the most, and what to say when you call your bank.
